historical_timeline.summary: Born in St. Francis County, Arkansas, to sharecroppers.
Field work from the age of eight; beaten regularly by his father; little schooling.
Imprisoned in the Missouri State Penitentiary; learns to box; paroled.
Wins the world heavyweight title; holds it until February 1964.
Moves to Las Vegas; described as a heavy drinker.
Fights for the last time; later enters the International Boxing Hall of Fame.
Dies in Las Vegas; found on January 5, 1971; the cause is disputed.

claims.statement: Charles L. Liston was born in St. Francis County, Arkansas, to sharecroppers Tobe and Helen Liston. His birth date is uncertain: there was no birth certificate (Arkansas did not require them until 1965); he filed for one in 1953 giving May 8, 1932, which the Encyclopedia of Arkansas and the Scribner encyclopedia use with a question; his family's 1930 census record does not list him, so he was probably born no earlier than late 1930; his mother gave several dates; and other sources suggest 1927 or 1928.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The preferred date is the one he used for official purposes; the uncertainty is recorded and no year is treated as settled.

claims.statement: He turned professional in September 1953 and broke his jaw in a 1954 loss. He won the world heavyweight title in Chicago on September 25, 1962, with a first-round knockout, and lost it in Miami Beach on February 25, 1964, when he did not come out for the seventh round, citing a shoulder injury; he lost the rematch in 1965. His record was 50 wins (39 by knockout) and 4 losses; he moved to Las Vegas in 1966.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the long exposure to boxing and his active career in the index year.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Trauma-informed primary care for a 37-year-old professional heavyweight boxer who grew up in poverty with adverse childhood experiences, spent time in prison as a young man, and does not read or write, seen after a high blood pressure reading at a boxing commission check. The episode follows the 2025 AHA/ACC blood pressure guideline and the CMID hypertension monograph: out-of-office confirmation by 24-hour ambulatory monitoring before the diagnosis, baseline tests including urine albumin and an ECG, an echocardiogram for stage 2 hypertension, a single-pill combination of two first-line drugs, and potassium and creatinine checks; the AHA/ACC eligibility statement for competitive athletes with hypertension; alcohol and drug screening (AUDIT, DAST-10) with nonjudgmental motivational counseling, naltrexone for alcohol use disorder, and a structured safety assessment; why naloxone is not prescribed when there is no opioid use; ACE-informed history taken with choice and control; health literacy universal precautions (spoken and picture-based plans, teach-back, read-aloud consent); cardiovascular risk; and preventive care. It makes no claim about his real health and does not draw on the disputed circumstances of his death.

hpi.narrative: Sonny Liston returns two weeks after intake and is seen the same day by Dr. Lindqvist-Owusu. He wore the ambulatory blood pressure monitor for 24 hours last week, including a training session, and had an echocardiogram this morning. His intake blood tests were normal apart from a mildly raised AST and GGT, which were explained to him in plain words as signs that alcohol is affecting his liver. He has cut his drinking from about 25 drinks a week to about 18 by keeping a tally of marks on a card, but found the weekends hard. He feels well and has no headaches, chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations. He wants to know whether he can fight again this year. No thoughts of suicide.

hpi.narrative: Sonny Liston returns four weeks after starting amlodipine 5 mg and valsartan 160 mg. He has taken it every morning and can say what it is for and when to take it. He did not send home readings for the first two weeks: the clinic had asked him to photograph the monitor and send the picture, and the steps on the phone were confusing. Clear to auscultation

assessment.assessment: Ambulatory averages are well above the thresholds for hypertension (daytime 135/85 and nighttime 120/70 mmHg) and agree with his office readings, so this is sustained hypertension in the stage 2 range, not a white-coat effect.

A wall thickness of 12 mm with normal relaxation can be seen with heavy strength training, but concentric thickening with high ambulatory pressures most likely reflects hypertension, at least in part. It is mild, with normal function and no sign of another cardiomyopathy. A repeat echocardiogram after about a year of control will show whether it regresses.

Normal potassium, kidney function, urine albumin and thyroid tests, no bruits or radio-femoral delay, and no drugs or supplements that raise blood pressure. Alcohol is the one contributor found, and cutting down should help. Screening for primary aldosteronism is not needed now; it would be if his pressure proved resistant or his potassium fell. A sleep study is not needed with a STOP-Bang of 2.
Heavy drinking raises blood pressure, and reducing it is part of his treatment; I support Dr. Achebe-Whitford's plan.

recommendations: Start a single-pill combination of amlodipine 5 mg and valsartan 160 mg each morning: two first-line drugs, as the 2025 guideline recommends for stage 2 hypertension, with a calcium channel blocker as part of the first combination, and an angiotensin receptor blocker rather than an ACE inhibitor because angioedema is more common with ACE inhibitors in Black patients
Check potassium and creatinine in two to four weeks; if his pressure is still above 130/80 mmHg at four weeks, raise amlodipine to 10 mg in the same combination
Home monitoring with a validated upper-arm monitor with a large cuff and a talking, large-number display, two readings each morning sent to the clinic in whatever way works for him

Avoid diuretics for now, as boxers often dehydrate to make weight; avoid beta-blockers, which blunt exercise capacity and are not first-line; avoid decongestants, anti-inflammatory pain pills and stimulant or weight-cutting supplements
Lower-salt eating and reduced drinking, alongside his training
No bouts until his blood pressure is controlled; then clearance by the commission physician with his readings, and a blood pressure check before each bout. He can keep training meanwhile
Repeat echocardiogram after about a year of control to look for regression of the hypertrophy; lipids, glucose and urine albumin yearly
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Achebe-Whitford, who saw him the same day. The findings were explained to him out loud in two main points (his blood pressure is high and needs a daily tablet; he can train but not fight until it is controlled), and he repeated them back correctly. A letter for the commission physician will be written once his readings are at goal
